records.greek: Ἦν δέ τις ἀσθενῶν, Λάζαρος ἀπὸ Βηθανίας ἐκ τῆς κώμης Μαρίας καὶ Μάρθας τῆς ἀδελφῆς αὐτῆς.
records.gloss: Was now a certain [one] being ill, Lazarus from Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha the sister of her.

L.1: Now a certain [man] was ill, Lazarus from Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha her sister.

R.1: Lazarus, a man from Bethany, was sick. Bethany was a village near Jerusalem, where Mary and her sister Martha lived.

decisions.choice: Bethany: the village on the Mount of Olives, less than two miles from Jerusalem
alternatives: Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John baptized (1:28)
decisions.reason: John places this Bethany about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem (11:18), a little under two miles. It is the village on the road to the Mount of Olives where Jesus stayed in his last week (Mark 11:1, 11; 14:3). It is not the Bethany beyond the Jordan (1:28), where Jesus is staying now (10:40); the sisters have to send word across the river to him (11:3).

decisions.choice: Lazarus: a Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, meaning "God has helped"
alternatives: the poor man of the parable in Luke 16:19-31
decisions.reason: The name was common. The poor man in Jesus's parable has the same name, but he is a figure in a story; this Lazarus is a real man with a home and two sisters. John does not draw attention to the meaning of the name.

decisions.choice: from Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha: two phrases naming one place
alternatives: two different places, his birthplace and his home
decisions.reason: The second phrase explains the first: Bethany is identified as the sisters' village, as though the reader already knows them better than Lazarus. Luke tells of Jesus as a guest in the home of Martha and her sister Mary (Luke 10:38-42). Verse 2 then says how Lazarus is related to them.

decisions.choice: ill: sick, weak from illness
decisions.reason: The verb means to be weak, and is the usual word for being sick, as of the official's son (4:46). The same word and its noun run through verses 1-6, so the opening sets the problem the whole story answers.

decisions.choice: A certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany
alternatives: There was a man named Lazarus who was ill
decisions.reason: The Greek states the illness first and then names the man; Balanced keeps that order, as Literal does.

decisions.choice: Bethany was a village near Jerusalem
alternatives: Bethany, the village of Mary and Martha
decisions.reason: Readable says where Bethany was, from 11:18, so that a young reader does not confuse it with the Bethany beyond the Jordan of 1:28 (meaning decision m1). It uses "sick", the everyday word, where Literal and Balanced say "ill".

records.heading: The death of Lazarus

records.greek: ἦν δὲ Μαριὰμ ἡ ἀλείψασα τὸν κύριον μύρῳ καὶ ἐκμάξασα τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ ταῖς θριξὶν αὐτῆς, ἧς ὁ ἀδελφὸς Λάζαρος ἠσθένει.
records.gloss: Was now Mary the [one] having anointed the Lord with perfume and having wiped the feet of him with the hairs of her, whose the brother Lazarus was ill.

L.2: Now Mary was the [woman] who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil and wiped His feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.

R.2: (Mary is the woman who later poured perfume on the Lord's feet and wiped them with her hair. Her brother Lazarus was the one who was sick.)

decisions.choice: who anointed: an act John tells later (12:1-8), by which his readers already know her
alternatives: an anointing that had already happened before this point in the story
the anointing by a sinful woman in Galilee (Luke 7:36-50)
decisions.reason: The past participles are past from the writer's point of view, not from the time of the story. John identifies Mary by the anointing at Bethany, which he narrates in 12:1-8, so he assumes his readers know the story; Mark and Matthew tell it without naming the woman (Mark 14:3-9; Matthew 26:6-13). Luke's account of a woman who wet Jesus's feet with her tears is a different event, in Galilee, with a different woman.

decisions.choice: the Lord: the narrator's title for Jesus
decisions.reason: In the narrative John sometimes calls Jesus "the Lord" (4:1; 6:23; 20:20), writing as one who knows him as the risen Lord (20:18, 28). Here it stands in a comment to the reader, not in a character's mouth.

decisions.choice: perfumed oil on the feet, wiped with her hair: a costly act of devotion
alternatives: an ordinary courtesy to a guest
decisions.reason: In 12:3 the oil is a pound of pure nard, worth about a year's wages (12:5). Guests' feet were washed with water; pouring perfume on them and wiping them with one's own hair went far beyond hospitality.

decisions.choice: whose brother Lazarus was ill: the aside returns to the sick man of verse 1
decisions.reason: The relative clause ties the comment back to the story: the sick Lazarus is Mary's brother, and so Martha's (verse 1). That explains why the sisters send to Jesus in verse 3.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "you" when the sisters and the disciples speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: parentheses; later; the Lord's feet
decisions.reason: Readable marks the comment as an aside in parentheses and adds "later", since the anointing is told in 12:1-8 (meaning decision m1). It says the perfume was poured on his feet, as 12:3 says, which keeps a young reader from picturing his head.

records.greek: ἀπέστειλαν οὖν αἱ ἀδελφαὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγουσαι· Κύριε, ἴδε ὃν φιλεῖς ἀσθενεῖ.
records.gloss: Sent therefore the sisters to him saying, "Lord, see, whom you love is ill."

L.3: So the sisters sent to Him, saying, "Lord, look, [the one] whom You love is ill."

R.3: So the sisters sent a message to Jesus. It said, "Lord, the friend You love is sick."

decisions.choice: a report that leaves the request unspoken
alternatives: a direct request that he come
news only, with no request implied
decisions.reason: The sisters do not ask Jesus to come or to heal; they tell him the need and leave it with him, as his mother did at Cana ("they have no wine", 2:3). The way they name Lazarus, as the one Jesus loves, is their appeal.

decisions.choice: love: the love of close friendship
alternatives: a lesser, merely human affection than the love of 11:5
decisions.reason: This verb is related to the word "friend", which Jesus uses of Lazarus in 11:11. In verse 5 John uses the other common verb for love of the same family, and the onlookers use this one again in 11:36. John uses both verbs of the Father's love for the Son (3:35; 5:20), so here they mean the same thing.

decisions.choice: Lord: the address of those who believe in him
decisions.reason: The sisters know Jesus and trust him; Martha will confess him as the Christ (11:27). As with his disciples (6:68), their word for him is "Lord".

decisions.choice: sent him a message (B); the friend you love (R); look omitted (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "sent"; Balanced and Readable say what was sent. The word "look" calls for attention; Readable lets the plain sentence carry the urgency, and says "friend" so that a young reader knows who is meant (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἀκούσας δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Αὕτη ἡ ἀσθένεια οὐκ ἔστιν πρὸς θάνατον ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ δι’ αὐτῆς.
records.gloss: Having heard now the Jesus said, "This the illness not is toward death but for the glory of the God, that may be glorified the Son of the God through it."

L.4: And having heard [it], Jesus said, "This illness is not toward death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."

R.4: When Jesus heard about it, He said, "This sickness will not end with death. It has happened for the glory of God. Through it, the Son of God will be glorified."

decisions.choice: not toward death: death will not be where this illness ends
alternatives: the illness is not fatal; Lazarus will not die
decisions.reason: The phrase names the goal or outcome of the illness; 1 John 5:16-17 uses the same phrase of a sin that leads to death. Lazarus does die (11:14), so Jesus is not promising that he will recover. He is saying that death will not have the last word: the illness will end in Lazarus being raised. Those who heard it could take it more simply, and the story shows them grieving (11:21, 32).

decisions.choice: for the glory of God: the illness will be the occasion for God's glory to be seen
alternatives: for people to give God praise
decisions.reason: At Cana Jesus revealed his glory in the first sign (2:11); here the last and greatest sign will show the glory of God, as Jesus reminds Martha at the tomb (11:40). Compare 9:3, where the man was born blind so that the works of God might be revealed in him.

decisions.choice: the Son of God glorified: through the sign, and through the death to which it leads
alternatives: honored by people because of the miracle only
decisions.reason: In John, Jesus is glorified above all in his death and resurrection (12:23; 13:31-32; 17:1). The raising of Lazarus shows who he is, and it also leads the council to plan his death (11:47-53). John's reader can hear both senses in the word.

decisions.choice: through it: through the illness
decisions.reason: The pronoun matches the word for illness. What looks like disaster is the means by which the Son is glorified.

decisions.choice: is not going to end in death (B); will not end with death (R)
decisions.reason: "Unto death" is no longer ordinary English, and "not fatal" would say that Lazarus will not die, which is not the sense (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable say where the illness ends. "Glory" and "glorified" stay at every level as key terms.

records.greek: ἠγάπα δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὴν Μάρθαν καὶ τὴν ἀδελφὴν αὐτῆς καὶ τὸν Λάζαρον.
records.gloss: Loved now the Jesus the Martha and the sister of her and the Lazarus.

L.5: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.

R.5: Jesus loved Martha, her sister Mary, and Lazarus.

decisions.choice: loved: the same love as in verse 3, said in the other common verb
alternatives: a higher, self-giving love, distinct from the friendship of verse 3
decisions.reason: John uses the two verbs for love side by side in this story (11:3, 5, 36) and both of the Father's love for the Son (3:35; 5:20). The change of verb here is a matter of style. The narrator states plainly what the sisters appealed to.

decisions.choice: a comment that explains what comes next
alternatives: a separate remark with no link to verse 6
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense describes a lasting love, and the particle marks a comment by the narrator. Placed just before "So ... he stayed" (verse 6), it tells the reader that the delay comes from love, not from lack of it.

decisions.choice: Martha named first, and Mary only as her sister
alternatives: Mary as the more important of the two
decisions.reason: In verses 1-2 Mary is named first; here the order changes. Martha may have been the elder or the head of the household: in Luke it is Martha who receives Jesus into her home (Luke 10:38), and in this story she is the first to go and meet him (11:20).

decisions.choice: her sister Mary
decisions.reason: Readable names Mary so that a young reader does not have to work back to verse 1.

records.greek: ὡς οὖν ἤκουσεν ὅτι ἀσθενεῖ, τότε μὲν ἔμεινεν ἐν ᾧ ἦν τόπῳ δύο ἡμέρας·
records.gloss: When therefore he heard that he is ill, then indeed he remained in [the] which he was place two days;

L.6: So when He heard that he was ill, He then stayed two days in the place where He was;

R.6: So when Jesus heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two more days.

decisions.choice: So: the delay follows from his love (verse 5) and serves the purpose he has named (verse 4)
alternatives: yet: he stayed in spite of his love
now: a mere resumption of the story
decisions.reason: The particle normally draws a consequence. John has just said that Jesus loved them, and goes on: so he stayed. The delay is not indifference; it gives time for what Jesus has said will happen, the glory of God (11:4), and for what will help the disciples believe (11:15). Throughout John, Jesus acts at the Father's time and not when others press him (2:3-4; 7:6-10).

decisions.choice: then, on the one hand: the first half of a pair completed by "then after this" in verse 7
decisions.reason: The particle looks ahead: first he stayed two days; then he said, "Let us go". The two verses are one step in the story.

decisions.choice: the timing: Lazarus may have died about the time the message reached Jesus
decisions.reason: When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days (11:17). If the messengers needed about a day to reach the place beyond the Jordan, Jesus waited two days, and the journey back took about a day, Lazarus may have died soon after the message was sent. John gives no exact times, so this is only a likely reckoning.

decisions.choice: So, at every level
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the plain "So" that John wrote, surprising as it is, so that the reader can see the link with Jesus's love (meaning decision m1). A footnote gives the reading "yet".

decisions.choice: Lazarus; two more days
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Lazarus, since "he" could be taken as Jesus, and say "two more days", since Jesus was already staying there (10:40).

records.greek: ἔπειτα μετὰ τοῦτο λέγει τοῖς μαθηταῖς· Ἄγωμεν εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν πάλιν.
records.gloss: Then after this he says to the disciples, "Let us go into the Judea again."

L.7: Then after this He says to the disciples, "Let us go into Judea again."

R.7: After that, Jesus said to His disciples, "Let us go back to Judea."

decisions.choice: Judea: the region around Jerusalem, where his life is in danger
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say "to Bethany" but "to Judea", the region where he had been threatened (7:1) and where they had tried to stone and seize him (10:31, 39). The disciples hear it that way at once (verse 8).

decisions.choice: then after this: two time words together, marking the end of the two days
decisions.reason: The doubled expression completes the pair begun in verse 6: he stayed two days, and only then he spoke.

decisions.choice: he says: a present tense in a story told in the past
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present to make a scene vivid (1:21; 9:12). The same happens in verses 8 and 11. It does not change the time.

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John's present tense (meaning decision m3) is kept in Literal; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This applies to "say" in verse 8 and "says" in verse 11 as well. The present in verse 13 is different: it stands in a reported thought, and every level turns it into the past.

decisions.choice: go back to Judea
decisions.reason: "Again" here means a return; "go back" says that naturally.

records.greek: λέγουσιν αὐτῷ οἱ μαθηταί· Ῥαββί, νῦν ἐζήτουν σε λιθάσαι οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι, καὶ πάλιν ὑπάγεις ἐκεῖ;
records.gloss: Say to him the disciples, "Rabbi, now were seeking you to stone the Jews, and again you go there?"

L.8: The disciples say to Him, "Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone You, and again You are going there?"

R.8: But the disciples said, "Rabbi, not long ago the Jews in the temple tried to stone You. Are You really going back there?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the hostile hearers in the temple who picked up stones to stone him (10:31)
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: The disciples refer to a particular event: at the feast of Dedication the people who surrounded Jesus in Solomon's colonnade took up stones against him (10:22-24, 31, 39). They mean that group, not the Jewish people as a whole; the disciples are Jews themselves, and so is Jesus (4:9). The leaders may well have been among them, but the disciples do not single them out.

decisions.choice: just now ... were seeking: a short time ago they were trying
alternatives: at this very moment they are seeking
decisions.reason: "Now" here looks back to the recent past, the winter feast (10:22). The imperfect describes the attempt that was cut short when Jesus escaped (10:39).

decisions.choice: and you are going there again?: a question of alarm
decisions.reason: The disciples can hardly believe it: going back means walking into the danger Jesus has just escaped. Thomas will draw the conclusion in verse 16.

decisions.choice: the Jews at the temple (B); the Jews in the temple (R)
decisions.reason: The word here means the group that tried to stone Jesus in the temple (meaning decision m1), not the authorities alone and not the Jewish people as a whole. Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to that place and that group, as 10:31 does, so that no reader takes it of all Jews.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς· Οὐχὶ δώδεκα ὧραί εἰσιν τῆς ἡμέρας;
records.gloss: Answered Jesus, "Not twelve hours are of the day?

L.9: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours of the day?

R.9: Jesus answered, "Does the daylight not last for twelve hours?

decisions.choice: twelve hours: the daylight, from sunrise to sunset, divided into twelve parts
alternatives: a full day of twenty-four hours
decisions.reason: People counted the hours of the day from sunrise, as in the parable of the workers (Matthew 20:1-12) and in John's "tenth hour" (1:39) and "sixth hour" (4:6). The hours were longer in summer and shorter in winter, but there were always twelve of daylight.

decisions.choice: a question expecting yes: the day has a fixed length that no one can shorten
alternatives: a simple saying about working hours
decisions.reason: Jesus answers the disciples' fear with a picture. His time is set by the Father; until his hour comes, no one can cut it short (7:30; 8:20). In 9:4 he spoke of working while it is day, before night comes.

decisions.choice: the daylight
decisions.reason: Readable says "daylight", since the twelve hours are the hours of light (meaning decision m1), and so prepares for the light of the next sentence.

records.greek: ἐάν τις περιπατῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, οὐ προσκόπτει, ὅτι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου τούτου βλέπει·
records.gloss: If anyone walks in the day, not he stumbles, because the light of the world this he sees;

L.9: If anyone walks about in the day, they do not stumble, since they see the light of this world;

R.9: People who walk during the day do not trip and fall. They can see by the light of this world, the sun.

decisions.choice: the light of this world: the sun, which lights the world by day
alternatives: Jesus himself, with no reference to the sun
decisions.reason: In the picture, the light of this world is daylight: someone walking by day sees the path. The words are chosen with care, though, for Jesus has twice called himself "the light of the world" (8:12; 9:5).

decisions.choice: the picture points to walking with Jesus, the true light
decisions.reason: Whoever follows Jesus will not walk in darkness (8:12); walk while you have the light, so that darkness does not overtake you (12:35-36). For Jesus himself, it means that while his day lasts he can go to Judea without fear; for the disciples, that they are safe walking with him.

decisions.choice: if anyone: a general statement about any person
decisions.reason: The condition is general, and "anyone" means a man or a woman. It applies to Jesus and to the disciples alike.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they see|he sees}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" includes men and women (meaning decision m3), so the following pronouns take the gender setting. Readable says "people ... they", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: trip and fall; the sun
alternatives: stumble; the light of this world (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable says what stumbling is and names the sun as the light of this world (meaning decision m1), keeping the word "world" so that the link with 8:12 and 9:5 remains.

records.greek: ἐὰν δέ τις περιπατῇ ἐν τῇ νυκτί, προσκόπτει, ὅτι τὸ φῶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: If but anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light not is in him.

L.10: But if anyone walks about in the night, they stumble, since the light is not in them."

R.10: But people who walk at night trip and fall, because they have no light in them."

decisions.choice: the light is not in him: the person lacks light within
alternatives: simply "there is no light for him"
decisions.reason: One would expect "there is no light around him". Instead Jesus says the light is not in the person, and the picture passes over into its meaning: a person needs light within. Jesus speaks of the eye as the lamp of the body in Matthew 6:22-23, and in John he calls people to believe in the light and become children of light (12:35-36, 46).

decisions.choice: night: the darkness, and the time when the light is gone
alternatives: night in the ordinary sense only
decisions.reason: In 9:4 Jesus said that night is coming, when no one can work. When Judas goes out to betray him, John notes that "it was night" (13:30). Night stands for the dark without Jesus, and for the hour when he is taken from them.

decisions.choice: trip and fall; they have no light in them
alternatives: stumbles; the light is not in him (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: Readable uses "trip and fall" as in verse 9, and keeps the words "in them" so that the shift from outward light to inward light (meaning decision m1) is still there for a reader to notice.

records.greek: ταῦτα εἶπεν, καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο λέγει αὐτοῖς· Λάζαρος ὁ φίλος ἡμῶν κεκοίμηται, ἀλλὰ πορεύομαι ἵνα ἐξυπνίσω αὐτόν.
records.gloss: These things he said, and after this he says to them, "Lazarus the friend of us has fallen asleep, but I go that I may wake him."

L.11: These things He said, and after this He says to them, "Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep, but I am going in order to wake him."

R.11: After saying this, Jesus told them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep. But I will go and wake him up."

decisions.choice: has fallen asleep: has died, spoken of as sleep
alternatives: is sleeping in the ordinary sense
decisions.reason: Scripture often speaks of death as sleep: those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake (Daniel 12:2); Stephen "fell asleep" (Acts 7:60); Paul writes of believers who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14). Jesus said of Jairus's daughter that she was not dead but asleep (Mark 5:39). The picture treats death as something one wakes from. The disciples take the word in its ordinary sense (verses 12-13).

decisions.choice: Jesus knows that Lazarus has died, and speaks of raising him as of waking a sleeper
decisions.reason: No one has told Jesus that Lazarus is dead; the perfect tense says that it has happened and remains so. He knows, as he knew about Nathanael (1:48) and the Samaritan woman (4:17-18). For him, raising Lazarus will be as simple as waking someone up.

decisions.choice: our friend: the friend of Jesus and of the disciples
decisions.reason: "Our" includes the disciples. The word is related to the verb for love in verse 3. Later Jesus calls his disciples his friends, for whom he lays down his life (15:13-15).

decisions.choice: fallen asleep; wake
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the picture of sleep and waking, as Jesus put it (meaning decision m1). If any level said "died" here, the disciples' answer and John's explanation (verses 12-13) would make no sense.

records.greek: εἶπαν οὖν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτῷ· Κύριε, εἰ κεκοίμηται σωθήσεται.
records.gloss: Said therefore the disciples to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will be saved."

L.12: So the disciples said to Him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will be saved."

R.12: So the disciples said, "Lord, if he is asleep, he is going to get better."

decisions.choice: will be saved: in their meaning, will recover from the illness
alternatives: will be saved in the spiritual sense
decisions.reason: The verb means to rescue or keep safe, and is used of being made well from illness (Mark 5:23, 28, 34). The disciples take sleep as a good sign: a sick man who sleeps is getting better.

decisions.choice: an irony John's reader can see: Lazarus will indeed be rescued from death
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of the salvation Jesus brings (3:17; 10:9). The disciples mean only that he will recover; the reader knows that Lazarus is dead, and that he will be brought back from death, though not in the way they think. John does not point this out, so it is a likely play on words, not a certain one.

decisions.choice: if he has fallen asleep: a real condition the disciples accept
decisions.reason: They take Jesus's words at face value. Their reasoning also suggests relief: if Lazarus will recover, there is no need to go into the danger of Judea (verse 8).

decisions.choice: get well (B); get better (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the disciples meant (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps "be saved" so that the reader can see the play on words (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: εἰρήκει δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς περὶ τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Had spoken now the Jesus about the death of him.

L.13: Now Jesus had spoken about his death.

R.13: Jesus meant that Lazarus had died.

decisions.choice: a comment by the narrator explaining a misunderstanding
decisions.reason: The pluperfect looks back to what Jesus said in verse 11. John often stops to explain what people failed to grasp (2:21; 7:39; 12:33).

decisions.choice: his death: the death of Lazarus
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to Lazarus, whom Jesus said had fallen asleep. Jesus's own death is in view in the chapter (11:16, 50-53), but not in this sentence.

decisions.choice: Lazarus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Lazarus, since "his" next to "Jesus" could be taken to mean Jesus's own death (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: ἐκεῖνοι δὲ ἔδοξαν ὅτι περὶ τῆς κοιμήσεως τοῦ ὕπνου λέγει.
records.gloss: Those but thought that about the rest of the sleep he speaks.

L.13: But they thought that He was speaking about the rest of sleep.

R.13: But the disciples thought He meant that Lazarus was just sleeping.

decisions.choice: the rest of sleep: ordinary, natural sleep
decisions.reason: The first noun comes from the verb Jesus used in verse 11, which can describe death; adding "of sleep" pins it to the sleep of the night. The doubled phrase shows exactly where the misunderstanding lay.

decisions.choice: he speaks: the tense of the thought as they had it
alternatives: a present tense used for vividness
decisions.reason: In reported thoughts and words Greek keeps the tense of the original: they thought, "he is speaking of sleep". It is not the present of vivid storytelling, and every level gives it as a past.

decisions.choice: a misunderstanding of the kind John often reports
decisions.reason: People in John take Jesus's words on the surface level: being born again (3:4), living water (4:11), food (4:33), eating his flesh (6:52). Each misunderstanding leads to a plainer word from Jesus, as here (verse 14).

decisions.choice: ordinary sleep (B); that Lazarus was just sleeping (R)
decisions.reason: "The rest of sleep" is unclear in English; Balanced and Readable say what the phrase means (meaning decision m1). Readable names the disciples and Lazarus.

records.greek: τότε οὖν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς παρρησίᾳ· Λάζαρος ἀπέθανεν, καὶ χαίρω δι’ ὑμᾶς, ἵνα πιστεύσητε, ὅτι οὐκ ἤμην ἐκεῖ· ἀλλὰ ἄγωμεν πρὸς αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Then therefore said to them the Jesus plainly, "Lazarus died, \v 15 and I rejoice because of you, that you may believe, that not I was there; but let us go to him."

L.14: So then Jesus said to them plainly, "Lazarus died,
L.15: and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, that I was not there; but let us go to him."

R.14: So Jesus told them clearly, "Lazarus is dead.
R.15: For your sakes I am glad I was not there, because what happens now will help you believe. But let us go to him."

decisions.choice: plainly: openly, without a figure of speech
decisions.reason: The word can mean boldness, but here it means speaking without a picture, in contrast with "fallen asleep". It is the word the crowd used when they demanded that Jesus tell them plainly whether he was the Christ (10:24), and it returns in 16:25, 29.

decisions.choice: glad that I was not there, so that you may believe: glad not for the death but for what it will lead to
decisions.reason: Jesus does not rejoice over Lazarus's death; he weeps at the tomb (11:35). He is glad that he was not there to heal the sick man, because the raising of the dead man will do more for the disciples' faith. The purpose clause stands in the middle of the sentence, between "I am glad" and what he is glad about.

decisions.choice: so that you may believe: that their faith may grow
alternatives: that they may come to faith for the first time
decisions.reason: The disciples already believe in Jesus (2:11; 6:68-69), yet John often speaks of faith that grows as people see more of who he is (2:22; 20:8, 31). The sign will deepen their faith before the testing of his death.

decisions.choice: but let us go to him: to Lazarus, though he is dead
decisions.reason: "But" breaks off the explanation: enough said, now they must go. Jesus speaks of the dead man as someone they can go to, as if he were still waiting for them.

decisions.choice: glad ... that I was not there, so that you may believe
alternatives: I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, that I was not there (Literal)
decisions.reason: English keeps "glad" next to what Jesus is glad about; the purpose clause follows. Literal keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: because what happens now will help you believe
decisions.reason: Readable says how Jesus's absence serves their faith (meaning decisions m2 and m3): what he is about to do will help them believe.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν Θωμᾶς ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος τοῖς συμμαθηταῖς· Ἄγωμεν καὶ ἡμεῖς ἵνα ἀποθάνωμεν μετ’ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Said therefore Thomas, the [one] being called Didymus, to the fellow disciples, "Let us go also we, that we may die with him."

L.16: So Thomas, the [one] called Didymus, said to [his] fellow disciples, "Let us also go, so that we may die with Him."

R.16: Then Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to the other disciples, "We should go too, so that we can die with Him."

decisions.choice: Thomas called Didymus: both names mean "twin", the first in Aramaic and the second in Greek
decisions.reason: Thomas is a Semitic name meaning "twin", and Didymus is the Greek word for twin. John gives the Greek name for his Greek-speaking readers, as he explains other Hebrew and Aramaic words (1:38, 41, 42), and he gives it again in 20:24 and 21:2. Whose twin Thomas was is never said.

decisions.choice: die with him: with Jesus
decisions.reason: Thomas answers the danger the disciples have just named: going back to Judea means that Jesus may be stoned (verse 8), and Thomas is ready to share his fate. "With him" could refer to Lazarus, the last person spoken of (verse 15), but dying with a man who is already dead makes poor sense.

decisions.choice: loyal courage, and an irony: it is Jesus who will die for them
decisions.reason: Thomas expects death and is willing to go. In the event the raising of Lazarus leads to the plot against Jesus (11:50-53), and when he is arrested he asks that his disciples be let go (18:8-9); they scatter, as he foretold (16:32). Thomas's words are brave, but it is Jesus who will lay down his life for his friends (15:13).

decisions.choice: Didymus (which means Twin) (B); the Twin (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the name as John wrote it. Balanced adds what it means, as John himself does for other names (meaning decision m1); Readable gives only the meaning.

decisions.choice: die with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The pronoun is taken to refer to Jesus (meaning decision m2), so it takes the deity_pronoun setting. A footnote gives the reading that refers it to Lazarus.

records.greek: Ἐλθὼν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς εὗρεν αὐτὸν τέσσαρας ἤδη ἡμέρας ἔχοντα ἐν τῷ μνημείῳ.
records.gloss: Having come then the Jesus found him four already days having in the tomb.

L.17: So Jesus, having come, found that [Lazarus] had already been four days in the tomb.

R.17: When Jesus arrived, He found out that Lazarus had already been in the tomb for four days.

decisions.choice: four days in the tomb: Lazarus was beyond any doubt dead
alternatives: four days: a detail with no further point
decisions.reason: In Judea the dead were buried on the day they died, because of the heat (compare Acts 5:6-10). So Lazarus had been dead four days, and the body had begun to decay, as Martha says in 11:39. No one could think he was only unconscious. The count also shows that Jesus came too late for any ordinary help (11:21).

decisions.choice: a belief that the soul stayed near the body for three days may lie behind the count
decisions.reason: Later rabbinic writings (Genesis Rabbah 100:7; Leviticus Rabbah 18:1) record a belief that the soul hovers near the body for three days, hoping to return, and leaves when the face changes. If the belief was held in Jesus's day, the fourth day would mean that all hope was gone. These writings come from centuries later, so it is not certain that the belief was current then; the point of 11:39 stands without it.

decisions.choice: him ... having four days: he had already been there four days
decisions.reason: The verb "to have" with a length of time is the ordinary Greek way of saying how long something has lasted, as in 5:5-6. "Him" is Lazarus, named in 11:1-14. The reckoning fits the story: the messenger's journey, the two days Jesus stayed where he was (11:6), and his own journey to Bethany.

decisions.choice: [Lazarus] (L); Lazarus (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says "him"; after "Jesus" an English pronoun would be unclear, so every level names Lazarus, Literal in brackets.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "you" when people speak to him; this applies throughout the passage. Literal keeps the Greek participle and needs no pronoun.

records.heading: The resurrection and the life

records.greek: ἦν δὲ ἡ Βηθανία ἐγγὺς τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων ὡς ἀπὸ σταδίων δεκαπέντε.
records.gloss: Was now the Bethany near the Jerusalem about from stadia fifteen.

L.18: Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia off.

R.18: Bethany was close to Jerusalem, only about 2 miles away.

decisions.choice: fifteen stadia: a little less than two miles
decisions.reason: A stadion was about 600 feet (185 meters), so fifteen of them come to about 1.7 miles (2.8 kilometers). Bethany lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.

decisions.choice: this Bethany: the village of Martha and Mary near Jerusalem
decisions.reason: John has already named another Bethany, beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing (1:28) and where Jesus has been staying (10:40). By saying how close this one is to Jerusalem, John makes clear which place he means, and why it was dangerous for Jesus to go there (11:7-8, 16). It also explains why so many came from the city to mourn (verse 19).

decisions.choice: was: the past tense of the story
alternatives: Bethany no longer stood when John wrote
decisions.reason: John tells the whole story in the past, so the past tense is natural here. It need not mean that the village no longer existed when he wrote; contrast 5:2, where he describes a place with "is".

decisions.choice: about fifteen stadia off: at a distance of about fifteen stadia
decisions.reason: The word "from" placed before the measure is a Greek way of giving the distance between two places (compare 21:8), not the starting point of a journey.

decisions.choice: about {{units:2 miles|fifteen stadia}}
decisions.reason: As at 6:19: Balanced and Readable give the distance in miles by default, rounded as the Greek "about" allows, and the units setting shows the original measure. Numerals are used in measurements. Literal always keeps the ancient unit.

records.greek: πολλοὶ δὲ ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐληλύθεισαν πρὸς τὴν Μάρθαν καὶ Μαριὰμ ἵνα παραμυθήσωνται αὐτὰς περὶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ.
records.gloss: Many now from the Jews had come to the Martha and Mary in order that they might console them concerning the brother.

L.19: And many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary, in order to console them concerning [their] brother.

R.19: Many Jews had come from Jerusalem to comfort Martha and Mary, because their brother had died.

decisions.choice: the Jews: Jewish people from Jerusalem and the country around, who had come to mourn
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Here the word means neither the people as a whole nor the authorities, but the friends and neighbors who came to comfort the sisters; verse 18 points to Jerusalem as the place most had come from. They are the same group who follow Mary to the tomb and weep with her (11:31, 33). Afterwards many of them believe in Jesus, while some report to the Pharisees (11:45-46). Martha, Mary and Lazarus are Jews too.

decisions.choice: to console them: the duty of comforting mourners
decisions.reason: Mourning for the dead lasted seven days (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13; Sirach 22:12), and friends and neighbors came to sit with the family and comfort them (Job 2:11-13). That so many had come suggests the family was well known and loved.

decisions.choice: had come: they were already there when Jesus arrived
decisions.reason: The pluperfect looks back from the moment of Jesus's arrival: the mourners were already in the house. This sets up the story that follows, in which they see what Jesus does (11:31, 36-37, 45).

decisions.choice: to Martha and Mary (SBLGNT)
alternatives: to those around Martha and Mary
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "to those around Martha and Mary", a Greek way of naming the sisters together with their household. The sense is the same, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Many Jews (B, R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the mourners present in the house (meaning decision m1), not the authorities and not the Jewish people as a whole. Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the people present, as 8:48 and 10:31 do, so no footnote is needed.

decisions.choice: from Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable says where the mourners had come from, which verse 18 implies. Some of them may have lived in Bethany itself, so this goes a little beyond what the verse states.

records.greek: ἡ οὖν Μάρθα ὡς ἤκουσεν ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἔρχεται ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ· Μαρία δὲ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ ἐκαθέζετο.
records.gloss: The then Martha when she heard that Jesus is coming met him; Mary but in the house was sitting.

L.20: So Martha, when she heard that Jesus is coming, met Him; but Mary was sitting in the house.

R.20: When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet Him. But Mary stayed at home, sitting in the house.

decisions.choice: that Jesus is coming: the words as Martha heard them
decisions.reason: Greek keeps the tense of the words that were spoken when it reports them, so "is coming" is what Martha was told. It is not the historic present of storytelling.

decisions.choice: met him: went out to meet him on the road
decisions.reason: The verb means to go to meet someone. Jesus had not yet entered the village (11:30), so Martha left the house and the mourners and went out to him.

decisions.choice: Mary was sitting: the posture of a mourner
alternatives: Mary refused to go out to Jesus
decisions.reason: Mourners sat on the ground or at home while friends came to them (Job 2:8, 13; Ezra 9:3-4; Lamentations 2:10). John does not say why Mary stayed; she may not have heard that Jesus had come, since Martha later tells her quietly (11:28-29). The two sisters act much as they do in Luke 10:38-42, Martha busy and Mary sitting.

decisions.choice: went out to meet
decisions.reason: Brings out the sense of the verb (meaning decision m2): Martha left the village to meet Jesus on the way.

decisions.choice: stayed sitting (B); stayed at home, sitting in the house (R)
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes Mary going on sitting while Martha went out; "stayed" shows the contrast between the sisters.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν ἡ Μάρθα πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν· Κύριε, εἰ ἦς ὧδε οὐκ ἂν ἀπέθανεν ὁ ἀδελφός μου·
records.gloss: Said then the Martha to the Jesus, "Lord, if you were here, not would have died the brother of me;

L.21: So Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.

R.21: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would still be alive.

decisions.choice: Lord: Martha addresses Jesus as her master
decisions.reason: Martha and her family are among those who love Jesus and trust him (11:3, 5), and the word leads into her confession in verse 27. As with Peter in 6:68, it is more than a polite "sir".

decisions.choice: if you had been here, he would not have died: a condition contrary to fact
decisions.reason: The construction states what would have happened if things had been otherwise: Jesus was not there, and Lazarus died. Martha is sure that Jesus could have healed him. Mary greets Jesus with the same words (11:32).

decisions.choice: grief and trust, with perhaps a note of complaint
alternatives: a rebuke of Jesus for staying away
decisions.reason: The words may carry some pain that Jesus did not come sooner (11:6), and some of the mourners say as much (11:37). But Martha goes straight on to speak of her trust in him (verse 22). She seems to think that Jesus had to be present to heal, although John has told of him healing at a distance (4:46-53).

decisions.choice: had you been here
alternatives: if you had been here (Literal, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the inverted form of the condition, which is natural in careful English and keeps the sentence short.

decisions.choice: would still be alive
decisions.reason: Readable says the same thing positively, which is easier to follow.

records.greek: καὶ νῦν οἶδα ὅτι ὅσα ἂν αἰτήσῃ τὸν θεὸν δώσει σοι ὁ θεός.
records.gloss: And now I know that whatever things you may ask the God will give to you the God."

L.22: And even now I know that whatever You ask of God, God will give [it] to You."

R.22: And I know that even now, if You ask God for anything, He will give it to You."

decisions.choice: and now: even now, after his death
alternatives: and now, as a weak link with no special sense
decisions.reason: "Now" sets the present, with Lazarus four days dead, against what might have been (verse 21). Whatever had happened, Martha's trust in Jesus has not been lost.

decisions.choice: Martha trusts Jesus completely, without saying what she hopes for
alternatives: she expects Jesus to raise Lazarus at once
decisions.reason: She may be hinting that Jesus could ask God to give Lazarus back to life now. But when Jesus speaks of his rising she thinks of the last day (verse 24), and at the tomb she objects that the body has begun to decay (11:39). So her words are more likely a general statement of trust, which leaves room for more than she dares to ask. The text does not settle it, and every level keeps it open.

decisions.choice: ask: the ordinary word for making a request
decisions.reason: Martha uses the usual word for asking something of a superior, the word Jesus uses for the disciples asking the Father (14:13-14; 16:23-24). When John reports Jesus's own prayers, he uses a different verb, the word for asking among equals (14:16; 16:26; 17:9). Martha speaks of Jesus as one whose prayers God hears (compare 9:31); she does not yet see all that he is, though his own prayer at the tomb shows that God does hear him (11:41-42).

decisions.choice: and now (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts begin "But even now", adding the word for "but". The sense hardly changes, so no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}; {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} for God
decisions.reason: "You" is Jesus, and "him" (Balanced) and "he" (Readable) are God, so all take the deity_pronoun setting. Balanced and Readable name God once and then use a pronoun, where the Greek repeats "God"; Literal keeps the repetition.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀναστήσεται ὁ ἀδελφός σου.
records.gloss: Says to her the Jesus, "Will rise the brother of you."

L.23: Jesus says to her, "Your brother will rise."

R.23: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise from the dead."

decisions.choice: your brother will rise: true of the last day, and about to come true that day
alternatives: only the resurrection at the end of the age
only the raising of Lazarus now
decisions.reason: The words could be the usual comfort of a friend who shares the hope of resurrection, and Martha takes them so (verse 24). But Jesus means more: he will raise Lazarus now, as a sign of the life he gives (11:4, 43-44). John lets the words hold both senses, as he often does with Jesus's sayings (2:19-21; 3:3-4).

decisions.choice: rise: stand up again from death
decisions.reason: The verb means to rise or stand up, and is a regular word for rising from the dead (6:39-40; 20:9). The noun "resurrection" in verse 24 comes from the same root.

decisions.choice: told (B); said (R); also answered (verse 24) and said (verse 27)
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 23, 24 and 27).

decisions.choice: rise again (B); rise from the dead (R)
decisions.reason: "Rise" alone is unclear in English. Balanced uses the phrase "rise again", which names rising from death; Readable says it plainly. Literal keeps the bare verb.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ ἡ Μάρθα· Οἶδα ὅτι ἀναστήσεται ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ.
records.gloss: Says to him the Martha, "I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day."

L.24: Martha says to Him, "I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day."

R.24: Martha answered, "I know that he will come back to life on the last day, when the dead rise."

decisions.choice: the resurrection on the last day: the Jewish hope that the dead will be raised at the end of the age
decisions.reason: The Scriptures promised that those who sleep in the dust will awake (Daniel 12:2; compare Isaiah 26:19), and many Jews of Jesus's day held this hope (2 Maccabees 7:9, 14). The Pharisees taught it and the Sadducees denied it (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). Jesus himself has spoken of raising the dead on the last day (5:28-29; 6:39-40, 44, 54).

decisions.choice: I know: a firm belief, but one that puts the comfort far off
decisions.reason: Martha does not doubt the resurrection. But she hears Jesus's words as a promise for the distant future, which does little for her grief now. Jesus's answer brings that hope into the present, in himself (verses 25-26).

decisions.choice: when the dead are raised (B); when the dead rise (R)
decisions.reason: "The resurrection" here is the raising of all the dead at the end (meaning decision m1), so Balanced and Readable say what it is. Literal keeps the noun.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "says to him"; Balanced and Readable say "answered" and need no pronoun. The historic present is explained at verse 23.

records.greek: εἶπεν αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή· ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ κἂν ἀποθάνῃ ζήσεται, καὶ πᾶς ὁ ζῶν καὶ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ μὴ ἀποθάνῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα· πιστεύεις τοῦτο;
records.gloss: Said to her the Jesus, "I am the resurrection and the life; the [one] believing in me even if he dies will live, \v 26 and every [one] living and believing in me not not will die to the age; do you believe this?"

L.25: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in Me, even if they die, will live;
L.26: and everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?"

R.25: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection, and I am the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even if they die.
R.26: And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?"

decisions.choice: the resurrection and the life (SBLGNT)
alternatives: I am the resurrection (a few early witnesses)
decisions.reason: A few early witnesses lack "and the life": Papyrus 45, one Old Latin manuscript, the Sinaitic Syriac and the church writer Cyprian. Nearly all other manuscripts, including the earliest papyrus of John (Papyrus 66) and Papyrus 75, have the words. A footnote gives the shorter reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: I am the resurrection and the life: Jesus himself is the life that overcomes death
decisions.reason: With a predicate, "I am" is ordinary grammar (see 6:35); this is the fifth of John's sayings of this kind. Martha placed resurrection at the last day (verse 24); Jesus answers that it is present in him now. The Father has given the Son to have life in himself and to give life to whom he wills (5:21, 26), and the raising of Lazarus will show it.

decisions.choice: two sides of one promise: the believer who dies will live; the believer who lives will never die
alternatives: both halves speak of the resurrection at the last day
the second half promises that believers living now will not die physically
decisions.reason: The first half speaks of bodily death: those who believe in Jesus will die, as Lazarus has, yet they will live, raised to life (5:28-29; 6:40). The second half speaks of a different death: whoever is alive and believes will never die in the sense that matters, cut off from God's life, because they already have eternal life (5:24; 8:51). Jesus does not deny that believers die; he denies that death can end the life he gives.

decisions.choice: lives and believes: one person, alive now and believing
alternatives: lives with the life Jesus gives
decisions.reason: One article governs both verbs, describing the same person. "Lives" most likely means is alive in this life, set against "even if he dies" in the first half. It may instead mean lives with the life Jesus gives, which comes by believing; the promise is the same either way, and every level keeps the open wording.

decisions.choice: never die: the strongest denial, for all time
alternatives: will not die forever (death will not be permanent)
decisions.reason: Two negatives stand together, the strongest way of denying that something will happen, and "to the age" adds "for all time". The same idiom is used in 8:51-52, 10:28 and 13:8, where it plainly means "never".

decisions.choice: do you believe this?: Jesus asks for Martha's own faith
decisions.reason: The question is personal and in the present tense. Martha has spoken of what she knows (verses 22 and 24); Jesus asks whether she trusts him now, and her answer is a confession of who he is (verse 27).

decisions.choice: even if {{gender:they die|he dies}}
decisions.reason: The one who believes may be a man or a woman, so the pronoun takes the gender setting, with the traditional "he dies" as the alternative. Balanced uses the plural "those who believe", which is already inclusive and needs no setting.

decisions.choice: even if
decisions.reason: The Greek states a condition, "even if", rather than a concession; every level keeps it, rather than the familiar "though".

decisions.choice: I am the resurrection, and I am the life
alternatives: I raise the dead and give life
decisions.reason: Readable keeps both nouns, since Jesus names himself, not only what he does, and repeats "I am" to make the two halves clear (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ναί, κύριε· ἐγὼ πεπίστευκα ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἐρχόμενος.
records.gloss: She says to him, "Yes, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the God, the [one] into the world coming."

L.27: She says to Him, "Yes, Lord; I have believed that You are the Christ, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world."

R.27: Martha answered, "Yes, Lord. I do believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God. You are the one God promised to send into the world."

decisions.choice: I have believed: a settled faith, emphatically her own
alternatives: I have just now come to believe
decisions.reason: The perfect tense describes believing that began in the past and still holds, as in Peter's confession (6:69). The pronoun "I" is written out and emphatic: whatever others think, this is what she believes.

decisions.choice: the Christ, the Son of God, the one coming into the world: the fullest confession of Jesus so far in John
decisions.reason: Martha gathers the titles others have given him: the Christ (1:41), the Son of God (1:34, 49), and the one coming into the world (6:14). John later says that he wrote so that readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:31); Martha says the same words here. She answers Jesus's question not by repeating his saying but by confessing who he is.

decisions.choice: the one coming into the world: the one God promised to send
decisions.reason: "The one who comes" was a way of speaking of the one God would send (6:14; 12:13, quoting Psalm 118:26; Matthew 11:3). John also speaks of the true light "coming into the world" (1:9). "The world" is the world of people, to whom he comes.

decisions.choice: the Son of God: the royal title for the Messiah, which the Gospel fills out
decisions.reason: Beside "the Christ", "Son of God" is first a title of the king God promised (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), as with Nathanael (1:49). John's readers know that Jesus is God's Son in a fuller sense (1:14, 18; 5:18-26).

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: The Greek has the article with the title, so every level writes "the Christ", with "the Messiah" as the setting's alternative (see the book's terms).

decisions.choice: I do believe
decisions.reason: Readable puts the perfect in the present, adding "do" to carry the emphasis of the written-out "I" (meaning decision m1). Literal and Balanced keep "I have believed", as in 6:69.

decisions.choice: the one God promised to send into the world
alternatives: the one who is coming into the world
decisions.reason: As at 6:14: Readable explains who "the one coming" is. Martha knew the expectation, so this puts nothing in her mouth that she did not know.

records.greek: Καὶ τοῦτο εἰποῦσα ἀπῆλθεν καὶ ἐφώνησεν Μαριὰμ τὴν ἀδελφὴν αὐτῆς λάθρᾳ εἰποῦσα· Ὁ διδάσκαλος πάρεστιν καὶ φωνεῖ σε.
records.gloss: And this having said she went away and called Mary the sister of her secretly, having said, "The Teacher is present and calls you."

L.28: And having said this, she went away and called Mary her sister secretly, saying, "The Teacher is here and is calling you."

R.28: After saying this, Martha went back to the house. She took her sister Mary aside and told her quietly, "The Teacher is here, and He is asking for you."

decisions.choice: secretly: privately, out of the hearing of the mourners in the house
alternatives: so that word of Jesus's coming would not reach those who might report him to the authorities
so that Mary could meet Jesus alone
decisions.reason: Mary was in the house with the people who had come to console her (11:19-20, 31). Martha speaks to her quietly, aside from them. John does not say why. The danger to Jesus near Jerusalem has just been mentioned (11:8, 16), and some of these same visitors later go to the Pharisees (11:46), but Martha may simply have wanted her sister to meet Jesus before the crowd did. In the event the mourners follow her anyway (11:31).

decisions.choice: the Teacher: the title Jesus's followers used for him
decisions.reason: John translates the title Rabbi as Teacher (1:38; 20:16), and Jesus says that his disciples call him "Teacher" and "Lord" (13:13). With the article it is the name the household used for him: Mary knows at once whom Martha means.

decisions.choice: is calling you: Jesus has asked for Mary; possibly an echo of the shepherd who calls his own
decisions.reason: John has not told us that Jesus asked for Mary; we learn it from Martha's words. The verb is the one used of the shepherd who "calls his own sheep by name" and is followed by them (10:3), and Mary rises at once (11:29). The link is possible but not certain.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for God or Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting: he, him and his for Jesus, "you" and "me" in his prayer (verses 41-42), and "you" when Mary speaks to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: Martha went back to the house
decisions.reason: Readable names Martha and says where she went: Mary had stayed sitting in the house (11:20).

records.heading: Jesus raises Lazarus

records.greek: ἐκείνη δὲ ὡς ἤκουσεν ἠγέρθη ταχὺ καὶ ἤρχετο πρὸς αὐτόν·
records.gloss: That [one] and when she heard rose quickly and was coming to him;

L.29: And when she heard [it], she rose quickly and was coming to Him.

R.29: When Mary heard this, she jumped up and hurried out to Jesus.

decisions.choice: rose quickly: she had been sitting at home in mourning and got up at once
decisions.reason: Mary had stayed sitting in the house (11:20). Mourners sat with the bereaved (compare Job 2:13), and the family received visitors there. She gets up as soon as she hears that Jesus is asking for her. The quickness is repeated in verse 31, where the visitors notice it.

decisions.choice: was coming: she set out toward him, and the story pauses before she arrives
decisions.reason: The tense pictures her on her way. Verse 30 then stops to say where Jesus was, and verse 32 tells of her reaching him.

decisions.choice: went to him (B); hurried out to Jesus (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say simply that she went; Readable's "hurried" carries over the haste of "quickly" (meaning decision m1) and "out" anticipates verse 30, where Jesus is still outside the village.

records.greek: οὔπω δὲ ἐληλύθει ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὴν κώμην, ἀλλ’ ἦν ἔτι ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ὅπου ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ ἡ Μάρθα.
records.gloss: Not yet now had come the Jesus into the village, but was still in the place where met him the Martha.

L.30: Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met Him.

R.30: Jesus had not come into the village yet. He was still at the place where Martha had met Him.

decisions.choice: a note of background: Jesus had stayed outside the village
decisions.reason: John pauses to explain where Jesus was. It explains why Mary had to go out (verse 29) and why the mourners, seeing her leave, thought she was going to the tomb (verse 31): tombs lay outside the village.

decisions.choice: the place where Martha had met him: outside Bethany, on the way in
decisions.reason: Martha had gone out to meet him when she heard he was coming (11:20). John does not say why Jesus waited there; it may have been to meet the sisters away from the crowd in the house, but the text does not say so.

decisions.choice: had met
decisions.reason: The meeting took place earlier (11:20), so every level puts it further in the past than the main story.

records.greek: οἱ οὖν Ἰουδαῖοι οἱ ὄντες μετ’ αὐτῆς ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ καὶ παραμυθούμενοι αὐτήν, ἰδόντες τὴν Μαριὰμ ὅτι ταχέως ἀνέστη καὶ ἐξῆλθεν, ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῇ δόξαντες ὅτι ὑπάγει εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον ἵνα κλαύσῃ ἐκεῖ.
records.gloss: The therefore Jews the [ones] being with her in the house and consoling her, having seen the Mary that quickly she rose up and went out, followed her, having supposed that she is going to the tomb that she might weep there.

L.31: So the Jews who were with her in the house and consoling her, having seen that Mary rose up quickly and went out, followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

R.31: The Jews who had come to comfort Mary were with her in the house. When they saw her get up quickly and go out, they went after her. They thought she was going to the tomb to cry there.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the friends and neighbors who had come from Jerusalem to console the sisters
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: These are the many who had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother (11:19), and they are named here by what they were doing: staying with Mary in the house and comforting her. They are mourners, not the authorities. Some of them later believe in Jesus and some report to the Pharisees (11:45-46). Martha, Mary and Lazarus are Jews as well, as is Jesus himself (4:9).

decisions.choice: thinking (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: The older manuscripts, among them the earliest papyri of John, say that the visitors followed Mary "thinking" that she was going to the tomb. Many later manuscripts read "saying", which makes the reason a remark they made to one another. The sense of the story is the same. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: to weep at the tomb: mourners went to the grave to lament
decisions.reason: Friends came to sit with a bereaved family and grieve with them in the days after a burial (11:19), and mourners went out to the tomb to lament there. The verb for weeping is the ordinary word for crying aloud in grief, the same word used of Mary and the mourners in verse 33. It is not the word used of Jesus in verse 35.

decisions.choice: she was going: what they supposed, told in their own present tense
decisions.reason: Greek keeps the tense of the thought itself ("she is going"); the sense is what they thought at that moment. They were mistaken: she was going to Jesus.

decisions.choice: The Jews who were with Mary (B); The Jews who had come to comfort Mary (R)
decisions.reason: Here the word means the mourners present in the house (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the people in the scene, as 10:31 does, so that no reader takes it to mean every Jew or the authorities. Readable draws "had come to comfort" from verse 19.

decisions.choice: cry
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday word for the loud weeping of the mourners here and in verse 33, and keeps a different wording for Jesus's tears in verse 35, as the Greek does (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἡ οὖν Μαριὰμ ὡς ἦλθεν ὅπου ἦν Ἰησοῦς ἰδοῦσα αὐτὸν ἔπεσεν αὐτοῦ πρὸς τοὺς πόδας, λέγουσα αὐτῷ· Κύριε, εἰ ἦς ὧδε οὐκ ἄν μου ἀπέθανεν ὁ ἀδελφός.
records.gloss: The therefore Mary when she came where was Jesus, having seen him, fell of him at the feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you were here, not would of me have died the brother."

L.32: So Mary, when she came where Jesus was [and] saw Him, fell at His feet, saying to Him, "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died."

R.32: Mary came to the place where Jesus was. When she saw Him, she fell down at His feet. "Lord," she said, "if You had been here, my brother would still be alive."

decisions.choice: fell at his feet: she threw herself down before him in grief and appeal
decisions.reason: To fall at someone's feet showed deep respect and was the posture of one who pleads or grieves. Mary is the one found at Jesus's feet elsewhere too: she anoints his feet in 12:3, as John has already said (11:2).

decisions.choice: Lord: the address of a disciple
decisions.reason: Mary and her family are among those Jesus loves (11:5), and Mary is the one who anointed him (11:2). She speaks as his follower, as Martha did (11:21, 27).

decisions.choice: if you had been here, my brother would not have died: a condition contrary to fact, the same words as Martha's
decisions.reason: Mary says almost exactly what Martha said (11:21): both sisters had believed that Jesus could heal their brother if he came in time. Grief and trust are both in the words. Unlike Martha, Mary says nothing more (compare 11:22). Her word for "my" comes earlier than in Martha's sentence, which may lay a little more weight on her own loss.

decisions.choice: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died (L); Lord, had you been here, my brother would not have died (B); ... my brother would still be alive (R)
decisions.reason: Every level gives Mary the same English words as Martha in 11:21, so that the repetition stays visible (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: Ἰησοῦς οὖν ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὴν κλαίουσαν καὶ τοὺς συνελθόντας αὐτῇ Ἰουδαίους κλαίοντας ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν, καὶ εἶπεν· Ποῦ τεθείκατε αὐτόν;
records.gloss: Jesus therefore when he saw her weeping and the [ones] having come with her Jews weeping, was indignant in the spirit and troubled himself, \v 34 and said, "Where have you laid him?"

L.33: So Jesus, when He saw her weeping and the Jews who had come with her weeping, was indignant in spirit and troubled Himself,
L.34: and said, "Where have you laid him?"

R.33: Jesus saw Mary crying, and He saw the Jews who had come with her crying too. Then He felt angry deep in His spirit, and He was very troubled.
R.34: "Where did you bury him?" He asked.

decisions.choice: was indignant: a strong stirring of anger
alternatives: was deeply moved, with grief or compassion
decisions.reason: Wherever else this verb is used it speaks of anger or sternness: Jesus "sternly warned" men he had healed (Matthew 9:30; Mark 1:43), and some at Bethany "scolded" the woman who anointed him (Mark 14:5). In wider Greek it could describe the snorting of a horse. So the word points to indignation rather than to sorrow alone, and it comes again in verse 38. Because tears follow (verse 35), it is often taken more softly as deep emotion. A footnote gives "deeply moved".

decisions.choice: John does not say what roused his anger; the setting points to death and its grip on those he loves
alternatives: anger at the unbelief shown in the weeping
anger at the mourners' show of grief
anger at the power of evil behind death
decisions.reason: Jesus is roused as he sees Mary and the mourners weeping at the grave of his friend. Some read it as anger at their lack of trust, since Mary has just said that he came too late (verse 32) and some will soon criticize him (verse 37). Others see indignation at death itself and the misery it brings, which he is about to overturn (11:25). John states the feeling without naming its object.

decisions.choice: in spirit, and troubled himself: within his own human spirit he was shaken
decisions.reason: "Spirit" here is Jesus's own inner self, as in 13:21 ("troubled in spirit"); verse 38 says the same thing with "within himself". The verb "troubled" is the one used of Jesus facing his death (12:27; 13:21) and of the disciples' hearts (14:1). With "himself" as its object it describes a deep inner agitation which he does not hold back.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the mourners who had come out with Mary from the house
decisions.reason: They are the visitors of verses 19 and 31, who followed Mary when she went out. They are mourners, not the authorities.

decisions.choice: indignant (L); deeply indignant (B); felt angry (R)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the note of anger that the verb carries (meaning decision m1), rather than turning it into sorrow. Readable uses the plain word "angry"; Balanced adds "deeply" for the force of the word. A footnote gives "deeply moved".

decisions.choice: the Jews who had come with her
decisions.reason: As in verse 31, Balanced and Readable keep the word John wrote and tie it to the people in the scene (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: Where did you bury him?
alternatives: Where have you laid him? (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: "Laid" means where the body was put; in plain English the question is where he was buried. The burial was in a cave tomb (verse 38).

records.greek: λέγουσιν αὐτῷ· Κύριε, ἔρχου καὶ ἴδε.
records.gloss: They say to him, "Lord, come and see."

L.34: They say to Him, "Lord, come and see."

decisions.choice: Lord: the address of Mary and those with her who knew him
alternatives: Sir, a polite address from mourners who did not know who Jesus was
decisions.reason: John does not say who answered. Mary had just called him "Lord" (verse 32), and the ones who show him the tomb are those who had come out with her. Some of the speakers may have been visitors from Jerusalem, for whom the word would only be polite ("Sir"), but in this family's company it carries the meaning Mary gave it. A footnote gives "Sir".

decisions.choice: come and see: the words of invitation from the beginning of the Gospel
alternatives: an ordinary phrase with no echo
decisions.reason: Philip said the same words to Nathanael (1:46), and Jesus invited his first followers in very similar words (1:39). There they invite people to come and see Jesus; here they invite Jesus to come and see the place of death. John may intend the echo, but the words are also the natural thing to say.

decisions.choice: They say (Literal); They said (Balanced), They answered (Readable); likewise in verses 38, 39, 40 and 44
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("they say", "he comes") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 34, 38, 39, 40 and 44).

records.greek: ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
records.gloss: Shed tears the Jesus.

decisions.choice: shed tears: a different word from the loud weeping of the mourners
alternatives: wailed, lamented aloud, like the mourners
decisions.reason: The verb means to shed tears and is used only here in the New Testament. Mary and the mourners "weep" with the usual word for crying aloud in grief (verses 31 and 33). John uses another word for Jesus: his grief is real, but it is not the wailing of the mourners.

decisions.choice: wept: a single act told simply; it may mean he began to weep
decisions.reason: The tense tells the event as a whole. It can also mark the start of an action ("began to weep"), but nothing in the context requires that.

decisions.choice: Jesus truly grieves, even though he is about to raise Lazarus
decisions.reason: Jesus knew what he would do (11:11, 23), yet he weeps at his friend's grave. The onlookers read his tears in two ways: as love (verse 36) and as helplessness (verse 37). The Word who "became flesh" (1:14) shares human sorrow.

decisions.choice: shed tears (L); wept (B); Tears ran down Jesus's face (R)
decisions.reason: Literal shows the meaning of the verb and keeps it distinct from the weeping of verses 31 and 33 (meaning decision m1). Balanced keeps the short, familiar sentence. Readable, which says "cry" for the mourners, describes the tears plainly so that the difference stays visible. No level adds anything else to the shortest sentence in the Gospel.

records.greek: ἔλεγον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Ἴδε πῶς ἐφίλει αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Were saying therefore the Jews, "See how he was loving him."

L.36: So the Jews were saying, "See how He loved him!"

R.36: The Jews who were watching said, "See how much He loved Lazarus!"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the mourners standing by
decisions.reason: They are the same visitors as in verses 31 and 33, who see Jesus's tears. They are mourners, not the authorities.

decisions.choice: loved: warm love for a friend
decisions.reason: This is the verb the sisters used in their message, "the one you love is ill" (11:3). John also uses his other verb for love of Jesus's love for this family (11:5). Both mean love; the onlookers see in his tears how dear Lazarus was to him.

decisions.choice: were saying, loved: several of them said it, and his love was lasting
decisions.reason: The tense of "were saying" suggests the remark passed among them. "Loved" is in a tense that describes an ongoing state: his friendship with Lazarus was long-standing.

decisions.choice: the Jews who were there (B); the Jews who were watching (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 31, Balanced and Readable tie the word John wrote to the people in the scene (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: Lazarus
decisions.reason: Readable names Lazarus, since "he" and "him" would refer to two different men in a short sentence.

records.greek: τινὲς δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν εἶπαν· Οὐκ ἐδύνατο οὗτος ὁ ἀνοίξας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τοῦ τυφλοῦ ποιῆσαι ἵνα καὶ οὗτος μὴ ἀποθάνῃ;
records.gloss: Some but of them said, "Not was able this [one] the [one] having opened the eyes of the blind [man] to make that also this [one] not should die?"

L.37: But some of them said, "Was not this [man], who opened the eyes of the blind [man], able to make it so that this [man] also should not die?"

R.37: But some of them said, "This man gave sight to the man who was born blind. Surely He could have kept Lazarus from dying too!"

decisions.choice: the blind man: the man born blind whom Jesus healed in Jerusalem (chapter 9)
alternatives: any blind person Jesus had healed
decisions.reason: With the article, "the blind man" points to a case they all knew: the man born blind whose eyes Jesus opened (9:1-7), a sign the people of Jerusalem argued over (9:16; 10:21). These visitors had come from Jerusalem (11:18-19).

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer yes: he could have
alternatives: a real question asking whether he could
decisions.reason: The form of the question assumes that he could have prevented the death. It repeats what Martha and Mary had said (verses 21, 32), but from people standing at a distance.

decisions.choice: a criticism set against the remark before it
alternatives: an expression of regret with no criticism
decisions.reason: John sets these words against "See how he loved him" (verse 36) with "but". The speakers grant his power and question his love or his reasons for staying away. Some hear real puzzlement rather than criticism; the words could carry either.

decisions.choice: Surely he could have
decisions.reason: Readable states the yes that the question expects (meaning decision m2), names Lazarus, and makes clear that "the blind man" is the one of chapter 9 (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: He opened the eyes of the blind man. Was he not able ...
alternatives: Could not the one who opened ...
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the healing first as a statement, then the question, which keeps the speakers' point clear without one long question.

records.greek: Ἰησοῦς οὖν πάλιν ἐμβριμώμενος ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔρχεται εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον· ἦν δὲ σπήλαιον, καὶ λίθος ἐπέκειτο ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: Jesus therefore again being indignant in himself comes to the tomb; it was now a cave, and a stone was lying upon it.

L.38: So Jesus, again indignant within Himself, comes to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it.

R.38: Jesus was angry again deep inside as He came to the tomb. It was a cave with a stone covering the opening.

decisions.choice: again indignant within himself: the same anger as in verse 33, still stirring as he comes
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in verse 33 (see the note there), here in a form that shows the feeling going on as he walks to the tomb. "Within himself" matches "in spirit" (verse 33): this is inward, not an outburst at those around him. It comes straight after the criticism of verse 37.

decisions.choice: a cave tomb: a burial chamber in the rock, closed with a stone
alternatives: a grave dug in the ground
decisions.reason: Families around Jerusalem buried their dead in chambers cut into the rock or in natural caves, and the opening was closed with a heavy stone against animals and the smell. Jesus's own tomb had a stone as well (20:1). Moving such a stone needed several people (verse 41).

decisions.choice: a stone lay against it: the stone closed the opening
alternatives: a stone lay on top of it, over an opening in the ground
decisions.reason: The words fit either a stone set against a doorway in a hillside or a stone over an opening cut down into the rock. John does not say which; the point is that the tomb was shut.

decisions.choice: indignant (L, B); angry (R)
decisions.reason: The same wording as in verse 33, so that readers see that the same feeling returns.

decisions.choice: over the entrance (B); covering the opening (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the stone covered, without deciding the shape of the tomb (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: λέγει ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἄρατε τὸν λίθον.
records.gloss: Says the Jesus, "Take away the stone."

decisions.choice: take away: a command to the people standing there
alternatives: a command to his disciples only
decisions.reason: The command is plural. Jesus has the bystanders do what people can do; only the raising itself is his. He does the same at the end (verse 44).

decisions.choice: opening a tomb after burial: a shocking request
decisions.reason: Once a body was laid in a tomb and the stone was in place, the tomb was not opened again except for a new burial. Contact with a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16), and the body would already be decaying, as Martha says next.

decisions.choice: Move the stone away
decisions.reason: "Move" is plain and does not assume that the stone could be rolled (see verse 38).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ ἡ ἀδελφὴ τοῦ τετελευτηκότος Μάρθα· Κύριε, ἤδη ὄζει, τεταρταῖος γάρ ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Says to him the sister of the [one] having died, Martha, "Lord, already he stinks, a fourth-day [one] for he is."

L.39: The sister of the dead [man], Martha, says to Him, "Lord, already he stinks, for he is four days [dead]."

R.39: Martha, the dead man's sister, said to Him, "But Lord, he already stinks! He has been dead for four days."

decisions.choice: already he stinks: a blunt statement of what she is sure of
alternatives: there will be a smell (a softer expression)
decisions.reason: The verb is the plain word for giving off a bad smell. The tomb is still shut, so Martha says what she knows must be true: after four days the body is decaying. Her words are blunt, and the story keeps them so.

decisions.choice: the fourth day: decay had begun and all hope was gone
decisions.reason: Burial took place on the day of death, and Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days (11:17). In a hot climate decay was well under way by then. A belief recorded in later Jewish writings held that the soul stayed near the body for three days; whether or not Martha thought of it, by the fourth day no one could doubt that he was dead.

decisions.choice: the sister of the dead man: John names her by her loss at this moment
decisions.reason: Martha is well known to the reader by now (11:1, 5, 20-27). Calling her "the sister of the dead man" here stresses that the one in the tomb is truly dead, and shows why she objects.

decisions.choice: stinks
decisions.reason: Every level keeps Martha's plain word (meaning decision m1); a polite word would soften what she says.

decisions.choice: But Lord
decisions.reason: Readable shows that she is objecting to the command just given.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῇ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Οὐκ εἶπόν σοι ὅτι ἐὰν πιστεύσῃς ὄψῃ τὴν δόξαν τοῦ θεοῦ;
